compression.title: Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs
compression.lede: is Wayne State University's labor archives in Detroit, "the largest labor archives in North America" by its own account, founded in 1960 as the Labor History Archives, its 1975 building a UAW gift (About page; ML record); its census record asks whose record it keeps, who holds it, and whether it keeps the losing side.

sentences.text: The Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs, at Wayne State University, 5401 Cass Ave, Detroit, is in its own words "the largest labor archives in North America" and "home to the collections of numerous unions and labor-related organizations" (its About page; the same sentence on its Research Guide and on DETROITography, the superlative on two Wayne State pages as the cards give them), which the maryleelabor census record enters as "labor archives; the largest labor archives in North America, in its own words; also home of the Wayne State University Archives" (ML record, reuther.wayne.edu).

Wikipedia gives the superlative for "the United States" and the extent as "over 75,000 linear feet of archival holdings" in manuscript, photographic, oral-history, audio and film media, "millions of primary source documents" in all (Wikipedia, citing East 1975); the census record finds the count "not stated in the saved text", the size of the holdings among what the saved text does not answer, and the period "not stated in the saved text; collecting since 1960" (ML record).

The building is named for Walter Reuther, president of the UAW and of the Congress of Industrial Organizations (Wikipedia), and the census record carries the entity's 1960 name, the "Labor History Archives" (ML record).

The census asks of every resource it records "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", enters this one under "Archives and custody: collections of papers and records of labor and the left, held for later readers" and under movement and party documents, "the record of splits" among them, with the archival collection as its evidence kind, and takes its question from #1725, *Ils ne sont pas marxistes* (ML record).

#1725 states the variable the question measures: "The decisive variable in the record is what happens to the losing position after the decision", and "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender" (#1725).

The library was "established as the Labor History Archives at Wayne State University in 1960, with the goal of collecting and preserving original source materials relating to the development of the American labor movement" (About page; Wikipedia, citing Pflug's guide of 1974 under the name Walter P. Reuther Library of Labor and Urban Affairs), its collections growing for over thirty years under director Philip P. Mason (Wikipedia), and the census record gives its lifecycle from 1960 to the Election Day closure of 2026 (ML record).

In 1975 the library "was constructed with funds given to Wayne State University by the United Automobile, Aerospace, and Agricultural Implement Workers of America, and through a supplementary grant from the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare", and "A later gift from the UAW funded the construction of the library's Leonard Woodcock Wing, completed in 1991" (About page; Wikipedia, which gives the wing as over 26,000 square feet).

Wayne State University operates the library and is its owner in Wikipedia's infobox (ML record; Wikipedia); the census record gives the holder as "Wayne State University; the 1975 building was funded by the UAW and a Department of Health, Education, and Welfare grant, and a later UAW gift funded the Leonard Woodcock Wing (1991)" and tags it "NOT the UAW's own archive: a Wayne State University library, though the UAW funded its building" (ML record).

The archive reads it as "a university holder whose building was funded by the union whose records it keeps" (ML record, ml_reading), the holder of whom #1725's second condition asks "standing independent of the executive" (#1725).

The library "serves as the official archival repository" for eleven unions, the Industrial Workers of the World, the UAW and the United Farm Workers among them (Wikipedia, citing Mason 1982), and its site groups its collections as "AFSCME AFT ALPA Damon J. Keith IWW JCA MDA NALC SEIU SWE UAW UFW WSU" under headings such as "Labor unions--Records and correspondence" (reuther.wayne.edu).

In August 2026 it opened an addition to the UAW Education Department Records, "one of the most essential collections from the union’s archival holdings" (reuther.wayne.edu), which the census record carries among its holdings (ML record).

The census record states whose record it keeps as "the records of unions and labor-related organizations, with Detroit's political and community life, civil rights and women's workplace struggles" and what it records as "original source materials relating to the development of the American labor movement" (ML record), and the Capture Registry heads its reading of the composition "THE CUSTODIAN OF THE UNIONS' OWN RECORDS" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

Beyond the unions' own records Wikipedia lists material of the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Coalition of Black Trade Unionists and the Workers Defense League; "personal papers from labor activists and union leaders", among them James and Grace Lee Boggs, Jessie and Martin Glaberman and Raya Dunayevskaya; oral histories of "union leaders and rank-and-file members"; and collections that "document the lives of working people and were not created by labor unions" (Wikipedia).

Its collection strengths "extend to the political and community life of urban and metropolitan Detroit, the civil rights movement in Michigan and nationally, and women's struggles in the workplace" (About page), with Detroit's community life, the papers of Mel Ravitz, Jerome Cavanagh and Coleman Young and the collections of the Society of Women Engineers (Wikipedia) and "a treasure trove of Detroit maps" (DETROITography), the census record's coverage being "the American labor movement; urban and metropolitan Detroit; the civil rights movement in Michigan and nationally" (ML record).

It is also the home of the Wayne State University Archives, established by the Board of Governors in 1958 and dating from the institution's founding as the Detroit Medical College in 1868 (About page; Wikipedia), and the census record tags it "NOT limited to labor" (ML record).

Whether it keeps the losing side the census record enters as "not recorded", lists among what the saved text does not answer "whether the collections keep the records of union opposition caucuses, dissent or expulsions", and holds that "whether a defeated caucus's papers are held beside an executive's is a question for its finding aids, unread here" (ML record).

The Capture Registry records the same gap in the composition and in the pages: "#1725 asks of such an archive whether it keeps the records of the oppositions inside the unions it holds; neither the composition nor the saved pages say" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

In the left's record, by #1725's account, a critique "gets settled by vote, verdict or decree, with the losing position carried into nothing that follows. Or it leaves with the people who hold it"; the SDS record survives "because the winning side wrote it down"; "Where a minority is denied its own public organ, the record shows exit as its only remaining move"; where the Reasoner's editors kept their journal "the critique kept an organ and found a wider field"; and "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority, so it is never sublated" (#1725).

The library "collects and facilitates access to historical documentary evidence in order to inspire academic research, serve the information needs of the community, and build knowledge at Wayne State University", donation governed by its Collection Policy (About page), its method in the census record "deposit and donation of organizational records and papers under a collection policy; finding aids; oral history" (ML record); the policy of 16 December 2014, a second attachment named "Good faith Efforts_public.pdf" and the mission statements are linked and unsaved (About page; ML record), and the site's menu offers Donating Materials and Oral History (reuther.wayne.edu).

The archive's account of custody bears on the class: "a custodian can keep the conditions for another's" turn (#1679), "custody decisions made about infrastructure are decisions made about meaning" (#1426), and "Archivists maintain records" is among the labor by which "Ontological capital is produced" (#1634).

Its ethic of custody is the obelus: "the custodian's suspicion must never be allowed to become the text's disappearance, because the custodian might be wrong, and the only insurance against a wrong custodian is that his judgments remain visible and his materials remain present" (#1068).

For the left's own papers the archive gives custody as a mechanism of loss: in #843 the loss of Marx's Second Manuscript has "archival custody" as its identifiable mechanism; Marx's papers passed "to Engels, then to the SPD's Berlin archives, then to David Riazanov's Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow", "Custodial modification of Marx's unpublished manuscripts is a documented pattern", and "a notebook lost in custody is the nineteenth-century form of registry severance" (#1066); #1067 sets the practice, "Reconstruct what custody lost, under stated constraints, with the falsifier attached", and the test of "custodial promise and custodial performance" for "an institution publicly charged with continuity" (#1067).

The records that outlasted suppression, in #1094's seven historical patterns, relied on "portable objects, independent custodians, multiple discovery routes, and an auditable record of loss" (#1094), independence failing where copies share "one administrator, registrar, hosting account or billing relationship" (#1435).

"The collections housed in the Reuther Library are freely open to the public. Appointments are not required"; out-of-town patrons are advised to contact the Reference Archivist in advance, a research appointment is made through Kristen Chinery, the reading room keeps weekday hours and closes on weekends and university holidays, and patrons are encouraged to search before visiting (About page); the census record gives access as "collections freely open to the public; reading room without appointment" and the hours as a stated limit (ML record).

Its collections are described by finding aids, "descriptions of archival collections that help researchers locate relevant materials", searched in ArchivesSpace, Digital Collections and the Library Catalog (reuther.wayne.edu; the Research Guide), the collection with its finding aid being the census record's unit; QuickSearch was retired on 17 August 2026 and "our collections can be searched separately using the tabbed search box near the top of our website" while discovery is integrated into Summon (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record), and through the finding aids the record answers "whether a named union or labor organization's records are held" (ML record).

The site's notice reads "All rights reserved" and the census record finds no license stated (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record); the library closes on 3 November 2026 for Election Day, and its latest post is dated 27 October 2026 (reuther.wayne.edu; ML record).

It is home to Labor@Wayne, the Centers for Labor Studies, the Employment and Labor Relations Program, the Fraser Center for Workplace Issues and the Michigan Labor History Society and runs APREL for K-12 and undergraduate use of archival materials (Wikipedia), and its podcast discusses "the six-week strike in 2022 of 48,000 UAW-represented academic workers across all 10 University of California campuses" (reuther.wayne.edu), which the census record keeps apart from its kind: "NOT a strike dataset" (ML record).

A journal article, "The Evolution of the Walter P. Reuther Library" (Project MUSE, 7 October 2025), gives it on the card as "part of Wayne State University" and "An innovative and ground-breaking ins...", where the snippet breaks off, and Wikipedia's article on it was last edited on 14 September 2026 (Wikipedia).

At its full name on 31 October 2026, a new address, the Overview named the library and the university with the library's site among its cards and, on the innocent reading, gave "its history, its collections and how to use them" and offered "to guide a visit": "An accurate account of the library's history and holdings, with one access rule stated against the library's own page and its funding by the union whose records it keeps not carried" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The registry records "THE ACCESS RULE RESTATED", the composition's "Researchers should schedule a research appointment in advance with Reference Archivist Kristen Chinery" against the About page's "Appointments are not required", and that "the composition gives the years of the building and wing without the gift" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31, under the title "AN APPOINTMENT ADVISED WHERE THE LIBRARY SAYS NONE IS REQUIRED; THE UAW'S GIFT OF THE BUILDING NOT CARRIED").
